## How to Become a Remote Online Notary (RON) in Your State


Notaries have always been the last line of trust in a real estate closing — the person in the room making sure signers are who they say they are, and that the paperwork is legally sound. As more of that work moves online, Remote Online Notarization (RON) is becoming one of the fastest ways for notaries to grow their business, serve more clients, and get paid for the expertise they already have.


Here's the good news: becoming a RON notary isn't complicated. It's a handful of clear steps. Below is what the process typically looks like, plus a few real-world tips from notaries who've already started.


> Real-world tip:
>
>
> Because requirements vary by state, this guide covers the steps every RON notary follows. Use the[National Notary Association's state-by-state RON guide](https://www.nationalnotary.org/knowledge-center/remote-online-notary/how-to-become-a-remote-online-notary)
>
>
> to confirm the exact rules where you're commissioned.


### 1. Check Whether RON Is Allowed and What Your State Requires


RON laws vary by state. Some states require a separate RON authorization on top of your notary commission; others have specific training, technology, or recordkeeping requirements. Before you spend money on software or training, check with your state's commissioning authority (usually the Secretary of State) to confirm what's required where you operate.


### 2. Maintain an Active Notary Commission


In most states, you need an active traditional notary commission before you can apply for RON authorization. If you're brand new to the profession, becoming a traditional notary is your first step.


### 3. Complete Any Required Training


Many states require notaries to complete additional coursework before they'll authorize RON. Training usually covers:


- Identity verification procedures
- Remote notarization workflowa
- Electronic recordkeeping
- State-specific RON laws


> **Real-world tip:** Even if your state doesn't require it, we'd recommend taking a course anyway. It'll make your first few sessions feel a lot less nerve-wracking.


###
4. Choose the Right Technology


RON runs on secure technology that connects you and the signer over live audio-video. Depending on your state, you may also need an electronic notary seal, a digital certificate, an electronic journal, and identity verification tools.

> Real-world tip:
>
>
> Before your first live session, do a full dry run: check your lighting, test your webcam angle, and make sure your internet is stable. Signers get nervous about the process too so a notary who looks and sounds confident on camera puts them at ease fast.


### 5. Secure Any Required Bond or Insurance


Some states require a surety bond, Errors & Omissions (E&O) insurance, or both, before you can get RON-authorized. Requirements vary, so confirm what your state needs before you apply and budget for it as a cost of getting started.


###
6. Apply for RON Authorization


Once training and technology are squared away, submit your application. States may ask for proof of training, information about your technology provider, and bond/insurance documentation.


> Real-world tip:
>
>
> Processing times vary widely by state, so if you're targeting a specific start date, apply earlier than you think you need to.


### 7. Start Growing Your RON Business


Once you're approved, you're ready to take on RON assignments. For most notaries, this means serving clients who want the convenience of signing online, cutting travel time out of your day, and expanding how far your business can reach.

### The Bottom Line
